[b]My playtime:[/b] I played this offline, but i think it took somewhere around 12-24h to finish the game.
[b]Grindy Achievement:[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement:[/b] Yes (8 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement:[/b] No.
[b]Developer Response:[/b] No (last response is in 26 Feb, 2019).

[h1]Intro[/h1]
Hacknet is a hacking simulator game where you have to hack some ip address with the tools you had. Most of the hacking will be done through terminal although the game has some GUI that you can interact with.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Even though i said that you'll type your commands through terminal, it doesn't mean that you'll only have to look at it. There are some UI in the game that you can see, such as when you launch your tools or check the compromised system. I even think that the UI helped very well because i'm sure i don't want to browse all of the system directory from the command line; it took too much effort to type and check them all. You can also see the server location and connect to them without typing at all in case you forgot the ip or just too lazy to type the whole thing.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The game's story is mostly told through an exchange of emails and reading files in a server. You'll investigate someone who has been lost for a long time, Bit, while uncovering a hidden secret that causes his disappearance. The story might look decent, but i'm quite impressed with the visuals at the end of the story.

The game also has additional files in the servers that you hacked in. I like to read some of them (especially the short ones) since they are pretty funny.

[h1]The game[/h1]
As a hacking simulator game, the game simulates the terminal very well. The basic is pretty much the same (ls, cd, cat, etc) while there are some custom commands mixed in. The game also has an auto complete feature although it's quite limited; you can't do auto complete for stuffs in other directory. Well, sometimes it works, but sometimes it don't. The game also doesn't support complicated command with arguments like rm -rf (remove everything in a directory) even though the game has missions like this. The limitations are pretty acceptable to me though.

Anyway, if you have no idea with anything that i said above, the game will help you to learn some terminal commands. If you're in windows, it's the thing that popped up when you press windows+r and then type cmd, except that the commands are for Linux OS and the like. Like how most terminals are, there is a help command that you can use to recognize all of the available commands and if you didn't notice it like i did, the help command actually has paging in it; you can type help 1, help 2, and help 3 to check most of the commands in the game. Most, because the help command won't tell you anything about what does your .exe file do.

Beside the basic commands, you'll also have .exe files. These files are usually what is installed in your computer and can be basically anything, from a browser to your game. However, most .exe files in this game is actually a tool that is used for hacking. You'll know how the things work if you read the instructions, which is obviously stored somewhere else. You'll usually get these .exe files by going through some servers and copying the files to your machine.

In this game, you'll need to read a lot. By a lot, i mean a lot. Really. You might need to understand some complicated stuffs or just know the general knowledge and the game will punish you severely if you don't know what are you doing. I mistook proxy servers and port for a while and i thought that i need 4 proxy servers to hack in a server although it actually asked me to open 4 ports. I got confused for a while before i noticed my mistake.

Sometimes, the game won't tell you what to do and you had to understand everything by yourself. One example is when a hacker suddenly attacked me. I didn't know what to do at that point because the tutorial (yes, there is a tutorial) only tells me how to hack.

As i said before, you'll usually hack a server. You'll have a lead in a form of ip address that you need to hack in and you'll check what you need to do to hack it. The game will usually tell you whether you have to connect to a proxy, guess a firewall, run one of your hacking tools to open a number of port required to get in, or all of them. Sometimes, the server owner will notice your break in and a timer will show up. You must finish your hacking, remove your traces, and logout before it reaches zero or you'll get a blue screen. The strange thing is, the game is a bit "buggy" on this. If you leave the server while running your hacking tools, the hacking will still be ongoing and you can do your second attempt with a head start. The stranger thing is, if the timer reach zero by the time you finish the hacking (and you haven't logged out yet), the hacking will also be finished after you deal with the blue screen and return to the server. Well, there are actually some more, but these two are the only thing that i had in my mind for now.

Since you'll use a lot of hacking tools, you might run out of memories. Some hacking tools take more memories than the others so you can't use them all at the same time. This helps to make the game more difficult although there is one place where you have to "cheat" your way through because you will never have the time to get in in the first place [spoiler](the CCC Hacksquad Filedump)[/spoiler].

The game's story has a two branching paths that will converge in the end. The other path requires you to really know what you're doing though; i won't be able to make it in if i didn't read a guide beforehand. The game also has some commands that are not available in help commands that might be useful in these cases. These additional commands are told after you beat the game and is supposed to be an additional command in case there is a new update in.

You'll mostly play the game by accepting quests and finishing them. There is also a few points in the game where you can choose the missions that you want to do. Sadly, there is a place where you can't choose them all and it kinda saddens me since it left the place with unfinished tasks.

Since you'll be hacking a lot of servers, there are some optional places that you can go to and some places might have some secrets in it. I had fun locating a lot of new servers that are not introduced in the main story although i'm not sure if i got all of them; sometimes, the secret is so well hidden that you have to read really carefully.

Pros:
- Uses mostly real terminal commands
- 2 branching paths
- Lots of secrets to explore

Cons:
- Leaving the server during a trace is kinda buggy
- You need to read a lot

[h1]Conclusions[/h1]
This is a nice hacking simulation game to spend your time with.

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to play hacking simulation game, buy this. You might have to know a little bit about terminals though; you can actually play it without knowing it at all but it might give you a harder time, especially if you don't like to learn and read.[/i]

review_text_raw:
The best way to start the review is to mention that this is game is for everyone. It's designed to let even the least "techy" of the players understand the concept and how it works.

As someone who does quite a lot of work on command line on a daily basis, I can definitely say that the game is very friendly in that aspect, and that the developers did a lot of work on making it as realistic as possible, without having the players browse through endless 'man' pages of every command. And it has very positive effects. The simplification of the entire interface, of the commands themselves, makes for a nice introduction for people who never used it before, or for people who have some sort of irrational belief that the command line is only for "hacker gods". People who are already familiar with the command line interface on UNIX based systems will find some of the classic commands returning in this game.

It's not bad at portraying the way most of the black/gray-hat hacking is done. These days, the movies often portray hackers as some wizards who constantly type in various codes on the keyboard while looking at the 8 screen wall with various kinds of text/graphical output, analyzing them in mere seconds and breaking into NASA/CIA/FBI/KGB/<whatever else the movie's plot is about> servers. All that while looking cool. No, no and no. This is not how hacking generally looks like. Instead, as the game itself portrays, hackers merely use (or write) programs with specific purpose (such as PortHack) to do the work for them, while browsing through the Internet, listening to music &c.

Therefore, one could conclude that the game is pleasantly realistic. Yes, some things had to be cut short or ignored. Some tools could hardly work the way they work, or their principle was fixed many decades ago, but it's all excusable, seeing as the main point of the game is providing fun, not having the player spend countless of hours reading stuff on StackExchange and various documentation sites.

Graphics are not the amazing 4k ultra mega sharp masterpiece that in order to run you'd need the latest cutting edge graphics card. They are merely... good enough for the game. It relies heavily on the command line so there is not anything that you could do about it anyway. There are many different themes (packed in the x-server.sys) and each of them has a different background and music.

The music? That's entirely subjective. I did not try a lot of themes, but I could notice that in all of them, the sounds were primarily electronic. Some were pleasant and nice to hear, some were annoying. Personal preference, really. 

The game itself has many references to the real world. These references are based on various movies, games, stores &c. I personally find them as a small nice addition which may or may not give you that "AHA!" moment. Most of them are just hidden in various text files.

With that said, the story of the game is... decent. I do not wish to spoil any of its elements, but let's just say that it's not the most innovative one. It's not a game breaker. It servers well its function to drive the game forward, but don't expect some legendary cool story that will keep you on the edge wondering what will happen next. I did not play the game's add-ons and thus I can't talk about them. Perhaps they are better, or perhaps they are worse.

And now, comes the greatest problem I have found with the game itself. Exactly because the story is the way it is, the game feels too repetitive. It can get boring quite quickly, many times over. While playing the game, you generally have the same routine, hacking into another system (done on the same way almost every time), retrieving/deleting/reading a file, delete the logs, log out. Sure, there are tracers to make the process faster. The firewall analysis can be rather fun when combined with tracers, as you get to feel like some sort of a movie hacker trying to find the right combination while the time is running out. But everything else is, as said earlier, too repetetive and boring.

So when it all comes down to it: 

Gameplay: 6/10
Realism: 8/10
Story: 5/10
Bugs: 9/10 (not a single bug found, although that doesn't mean that one couldn't be there)
Graphics: 5/10 
Music: 6/10
Overall: 6.5/10

I would not recommend you to buy the game with its full price. It's just not worth it. But if you find it to be free, or on sale, and wish to indulge yourself into the world of command line and hacking, then go for it.

review_text_raw:
This is gonna be a lengthy review. I'll add a TL;DR at the bottom.

When I first went to view the page for this game, there were many questions that began flooding my mind. And now that I've played the game almost to its entirety, I think that I can answer most of these questions that interested consumers passing by may have. This game was a real treat, and I think that it deserves more attention than it's received.


[h1] Is Hacknet realistic? [/h1]

If you mean "realistic" as in "Is this game close to hacking in real life?" then the answer is no. This game is not realistic because it is fun and doesn't make you paranoid. You are in possession of a bunch of hacking tools that put up the kinds of graphics you'd expect to be running on computers in a 90's hacker film, and the way these tools work is by executing them and waiting for the flashy hacking graphics to stop flashing so that you can run another flashy hacker tool until you gain administrative system access. Granted, it's more complex than that, which is why this game is really enjoyable, but you're not going to be writing complex algorithms to overload proxy servers and bypass tracing measures. That's what the 90's tools are for.

That being said, this may be as close as gaming will ever come to realistic hacking. Because anything that tries to be precicely like real hacking that doesn't give you fancy hacker programs probably isn't going to be a very fun game. And this, again, is a fun game. The entire game takes place on a computer's operating system, and every hack you perform is done through this system. In addition, the commands you use are based on real UNIX commands, even if the commands are typically used to activate the previously-mentioned hacking programs. It's certainly more realistic than games where you push a button and your character goes [i]"I'm in" [/i] like Watch_Dogs and Quadrilateral Cowboy (That isn't to say that they're bad games, just that they're not trying to be realistic hacking simulations which, again, isn't necessarily a bad thing).


[h1] Is this game immersive? Will I feel like a hacker even if I'm not performing real hacks? [/h1]

Oh, yes. If you want to feel like the genius hacker that always appears in Hollywood films but rarely gets any time for actual character development, then this game is for you. The presentation of this game is great, and it really helps to sell that feeling of accomplishment that you get when you pull off a successful job. After about 30 minutes in, I had to re-check the steam store to make sure that I wasn't accessing a multiplayer hacking simulator. But nope, I was even able to play this game in airplane mode. As the store page mentions, there are very few things that break the immersion by being obvious parts of a video game. To complete a job, you email the client explaining that you've finished. To acquire a new tool, you have to copy said tool to your home computer from its rightful owner. 

And this immersive presentation goes a long way in the overall experience. I know that not everybody responds the same way, but I found certain parts to incite genuine emotion in a way that few other games have managed to pull off. Like when you're given the option to accept a job in which [spoiler]you have to euthanize a dying man by hacking his pacemaker [/spoiler], or when [spoiler]you run "OpenCDtray" on your own system and your real computer's disc tray opens and may potentially scare the hell out of you[/spoiler]. So even if you're using overpowered tools to open systems that nobody bothers to check, you'll probably still feel really good doing so.


[h1] Do I need to know coding or hacking in order to understand this game? [/h1]

No, you don't. The tutorial explains everything pretty well, and it makes sure that you understand how the systems work before even thinking about letting you out into the hacking world. No coding is required (I'm not even sure if coding algorithms is possible with the interface), and most of the game's difficulty comes with memorizing the commands and executing them at the appropriate times. That being said, if you don't know a whole lot about computers, the most difficult task will probably be [spoiler] getting your interface back after being locked to terminal mode by another hacker [/spoiler]. But if you experiment enough, then you'll ususally find the solutions to most of the challenges, and there are plenty of walkthroughs and tips out there if you end up getting desperate. But I was able to finish the game with little prior programming experience. If you know how to navigate a computer's interface or have downloaded and fixed mods on to other games, then you'll probably be fine with this game. Just, you know, don't delete important files or screw up on a trace aversion. I don't know if this game prevents you from screwing yourself over, and everybody's too scared to find out.


[h1] Is the game worth ten bucks? [/h1]

Yeah, I'd say so. You'll probably get around 10 hours out of it if you're doing the main story without any outside assitance, 14-15 hours if you're also doing the labrynths DLC. I'd say that it's not everybody's cup of tea; surely, your relative who spends all day exclusively playing [i] Fortnite [/i] would probably get turned off by this, but odds are you're at least mildly interested in this game if you're reading this review right now, considering that this game gets talked about as much as what brand of toilet paper you prefer when you're finished up on the toilet. So yeah, I'd recommend this game to anybody reading this review.


[h1] Oh, boy. It's one of those games that tries to sell its soundtrack as DLC. Is it good enough to warrant a purchase? [/h1]

I was honestly surprised by this game's soundtrack. Again, I understand that everybody has different tastes in music, but I found this particular OST track good to write and do homework to. It felt really good to listen to in-game while hacking servers and computers. The music is used as sort of an indicator on what part of the game you're currently at, and when the song changes, you know you're probably making progress. I found that [spoiler] Roller Mobster by Carpenter Brut [/spoiler] fit this game better than it did for HM2. That being said, I haven't purchased the soundtrack since most of it is available on YouTube anyways. And yes, it's ten dollars. Fifteen dollars for the main game and DLC soundtrack. So while I'll admit that the soundtrack is pretty good, I'd only spend the extra fifteen bucks if you like having the songs directly at your fingertips at all times.


[h1] TL;DR [/h1]

This is a great game that may be as close to realistic hacking as gaming will come while still remaining enjoyable. The presentation and aeshetic really add a lot to it, and you don't need to be experienced with programming or hacking in order to complete it. It's worth the money and gives around 10 hours of playtime assuming you don't mess up massively and have to start a new game. I'm gonna give this a thumbs up, and I wish it came out later so that I could put it in my favorite 2018 games list.

[h1] Do I need to know coding or hacking in order to understand this game? [/h1] No, you don't. The tutorial explains everything pretty well, and it makes sure that you understand how the systems work before even thinking about letting you out into the hacking world. No coding is required (I'm not even sure if coding algorithms is possible with the interface), and most of the game's difficulty comes with memorizing the commands and executing them at the appropriate times. That being said, if you don't know a whole lot about computers, the most difficult task will probably be [spoiler] getting your interface back after being locked to terminal mode by another hacker [/spoiler]. But if you experiment enough, then you'll ususally find the solutions to most of the challenges, and there are plenty of walkthroughs and tips out there if you end up getting desperate. But I was able to finish the game with little prior programming experience. If you know how to navigate a computer's interface or have downloaded and fixed mods on to other games, then you'll probably be fine with this game. Just, you know, don't delete important files or screw up on a trace aversion. I don't know if this game prevents you from screwing yourself over, and everybody's too scared to find out. [h1] Is the game worth ten bucks? [/h1] Yeah, I'd say so. You'll probably get around 10 hours out of it if you're doing the main story without any outside assitance, 14-15 hours if you're also doing the labrynths DLC. I'd say that it's not everybody's cup of tea; surely, your relative who spends all day exclusively playing [i] Fortnite [/i] would probably get turned off by this, but odds are you're at least mildly interested in this game if you're reading this review right now, considering that this game gets talked about as much as what brand of toilet paper you prefer when you're finished up on the toilet. So yeah, I'd recommend this game to anybody reading this review. [h1] Oh, boy. It's one of those games that tries to sell its soundtrack as DLC. Is it good enough to warrant a purchase? [/h1] I was honestly surprised by this game's soundtrack. Again, I understand that everybody has different tastes in music, but I found this particular OST track good to write and do homework to. It felt really good to listen to in-game while hacking servers and computers. The music is used as sort of an indicator on what part of the game you're currently at, and when the song changes, you know you're probably making progress. I found that [spoiler] Roller Mobster by Carpenter Brut [/spoiler] fit this game better than it did for HM2. That being said, I haven't purchased the soundtrack since most of it is available on YouTube anyways. And yes, it's ten dollars. Fifteen dollars for the main game and DLC soundtrack. So while I'll admit that the soundtrack is pretty good, I'd only spend the extra fifteen bucks if you like having the songs directly at your fingertips at all times. [h1] TL;DR [/h1] This is a great game that may be as close to realistic hacking as gaming will come while still remaining enjoyable. The presentation and aeshetic really add a lot to it, and you don't need to be experienced with programming or hacking in order to complete it. It's worth the money and gives around 10 hours of playtime assuming you don't mess up massively and have to start a new game. I'm gonna give this a thumbs up, and I wish it came out later so that I could put it in my favorite 2018 games list.

review_text_raw:
This is not a game I hate. However, much like that TIS-100 game, I was left completely clueless as to how to proceed, though nowhere near as quickly, thanks to an actual tutorial and being able to play a little bit of the game before getting stuck, as well as a help menu listing commands. As a child in the 80s, I spent a fair amount of time using DOS to find files, modify them, etc., and in college, I used UNIX for a semester, scoring an A. There isn't a day that goes by where I don't use a PC, unless something really weird happens, like a blackout. Therefore, I was more than a little surprised when I got so hopelessly dumbfounded by this game. Granted, this game is far classier than TIS-100.

This game actually has music, and it's quite nice, while TIS-100 had none that I found. TIS-100's manual was difficult to understand and quite daunting, while Hacknet is far more user friendly, and really appears to have a story and more purpose to it. That said, the game left me confused and stuck when I came upon a firewall. The game never covered how to deal with firewalls in the tutorial. I tried running a program I had just downloaded from another computer in-game, which let me access one port, but I couldn't access any of the other ports. I used every page of help to look up commands that could help me, and analyzing the firewall brought up a wall of letters and numbers that didn't seem to do anything, and selecting to "solve" the firewall didn't do anything, either. I checked every computer I had access to and found nothing else that could help me.

If I'm stuck this early in, checking a walkthrough or asking for help online will likely lead to me continuing my confused wandering without learning anything within the game itself. I should not have to rely on the Internet to learn how to play a game for fun...

I'm disappointed in the game, but only because I liked what I saw when the game was presenting things in a way that cleverly educates the player, but then it throws you a problem early-game that no amount of searching within the game itself appears to turn up a solution. The point where it figuratively drops you in the deep end of the digital pool with a cyber-anchor tied to your feet is where I lose any ability to appreciate the game beyond that point.

It's also entirely possible I lack the mental faculties to interact with this digital gaming experience in a fulfilling manner. If that's the case, then so be it, but I must represent the "mentally deficient" population and state that I do not recommend this game as a result.

review_text_raw:
To be fair Uplink is better. This game is good because you get to use the keyboard. Uplink is a hacking game where keyboard is not used, so the biggest flaw is now solved. Problem is the game lacks a bit of adrenaline. 

1) Most servers don't trace you, so you can just hang around forever.
2) Its not clear where you are connected too. Once you hack a place is there opened forever. You don't even have to disconnect.
3) You clear your logs but not the disconnected log, which makes no sense. In Uplink you have to clear logs at origin and destination, seems more realistic.
4) Its too easy to go up the ranking. 
5) In Uplink you had money to worry about. Upgrade hardware and buy software. In Hacknet all you get is reputation, that also have no impact besides gettings invitations.
6) The game does not allow you to accept more than 1 mission.
7) The storyline is a bit broken. I made 1 mission that lead to a hacker invading my computer, that leads to another mission and to another mission and basically you cannot accept other mission while the "story" is leading you in 1 way. That made me join an organization and now I cannot finish the old missions. Basically I lost 3 missions, cannot be played.
8) The game UI is a bit limited. I cannot open a file and an email at the same time. Which makes very annoying to take note to things. Althought I cannot complain much on that, as in Uplink I really had a pen and paper next to me all the time, in this game I never used real paper so far.
9) Uplink allow you to do other stuff, such as Stock Market, browse any server, etc. Hacknet is limited. You only get the servers IP when the game wants you to get. There is not freedom besides follow the story.
10) Uplink allows you to choose which mission to make, in the sense of choosing to be a good or a bad hacker. In Hacknet some missions presentation don't have more than 2 lines. You have to accept missions without even knowing what skills you need, what tools you need and what you have to do. Its really 1 path only. And if you try to get missions in different orders you lose them, just like I lost 3. UPDATE: Because of this 1 path only + cannot accept more than 1 mission, you can game over all the time. If you delete the wrong file, edit the wrong record, its finished. People call this bug in the forum, I call this lack of flexibility. In Uplink you could simply give up on a mission and pay a fine. If you delete a file you are suppose to upload, it shouldn't be game over, just some kind of punishment.
11) It uses Unix commands but limit them. For instance you have rm command but cannot be used to delete folders. Cannot download folders either.
12) Find it a bit weird that no special software is required to know when you are being traced.
13) So far the challenge of the game seems to be more about curiosity of the player. Meaning you have to look into every folder and file and read and see what you can find (be aware) rather than having a challenge on the hacking it self, such as limited time, required software, go throught LAN networks, etc.
14) You can hack a webserver, a main frame, a home pc or a cell phone, they all look the same, they all have same file structure, they are all hacked with same tools. A bit boring no?
15) Network map completely unecessary. Its just a harder way to find servers, if you are not going to use it to bounce like Uplink, why have that? Just a window with animated blue balls. A list with a search box and some favorites would do the job, or better, connect always using the line command, IP or name assigned by the user.
16) Once you scan a server and it reveals other computers connected to that, more "balls" appears and its a mystery why some are very distant and some are very close. The distance is based on what? It simple confuses the player as it adds a connection between them and with time the connections cross each other. Well, still trying to figure out why did it this way.
17) I'm already playing this game for hours and all I do is execute programs to open ports.


The good:

a) Very well done interface in the sense that keyboard and mouse usage is well integrated. The key here is keyboard. Its very nice to be able to play the entire game using keyboard only.
b) I like the fact that webserver have website with real images. Just because its a hacker game, it doesn't mean the "normal" internet doesn't exist. Although limited, I liked the www.cfc.com.
c) You can see an effort to bring interesting content to see around. Most servers have files that are not crucial to the missions, things you can read, chats, funny stuff. That really adds to the game and was one of the things I feel lacking in Uplink. Perhaps this is one of the reason a lot of servers don't have tracing mechanism, so you don't have time pressure all the time.
d) Not having time pressure all the time is good, but also removed money pressure and other stuff, which is left it a bit unbalanced.
e) Nice animations. The screens change a lot. Its not the same interface all the time.

This is an extremely fun game, don't get me wrong, but I have two very major issues with it (especially the second one) that have prompted me to leave a negative review.  I very rarely review games on Steam, and only review the ones about which I am most passionately moved, positively or negatively.  In this case, negatively.  In contrast to my usual, I have enabled comments on this review -- feel free to state your feedback, whether you agree with me or not, just please remain respectful to me, the developers, other commenters, and anyone else as applicable.

There's a "TL;DR" at the end if you're lazy.

I'll start positive.  This game is crazy fun.  It is probably the funnest hacking-themed game I've ever played, and I've played a lot of them.  It was fun and helpful to see some things I recognize from real life, such as the default system port numbers being accurate and the existence of a few UNIX commands (my main OS has been FreeBSD for years, and my experience with UNIX helped with the gameplay in a way that felt good).  I liked seeing the C# source code and realizing it was actual, real C# source code that would probably work if the LESS_THAN was properly changed to a "<" sign, etc (C# is my main dev language, always a plus to see it referenced in a game at all).  That was cool, and I'll probably compile it later to have that tool on my PC for real (don't comment about the related real life security to this -- I assure you I already know, and it's just for fun).  The pacing was really good, and I got hooked fast.  So fast that I immediately bought the DLC, soundtrack, and DLC soundtrack for myself, then bought the game and DLC for both my wife and her boyfriend also.  Despite my negative review, I don't regret this decision at all, it's a very, very fun game.  Oh, the event thing that I can't discuss without giving spoilers, but well, the one where you need to get that thing back, that was super fun!  (Unimportant to the review and a spoiler:) I instinctively [spoiler]jumped to my host and forkbombed, apparently I was supposed to kill his forkbomb instead, oh well... I had already made a backup of that file just in case[/spoiler].  But anyway, the game was extremely fun, looks great, the music is great, and I'm excited to keep playing and see where things take me.

But there are two issues which were severe enough that they prompted me to leave a negative review despite all this.

The first issue isn't so bad and is easily rectified: This game is the pinnacle of Hollywood-style hacking.  It does it very well, and it references real hacking concepts in the game's flavor text and other areas.  Some tools are named the same as real ones, and you will probably learn a few real UNIX system port numbers, but that's about where the realism ends.  Oh, and [b]this wouldn't bother me in the slightest[/b] -- I love Hollywood-style hacking sim games! -- but it clearly says this in the "Features" section in the game's Steam page description, which to me is [u]blatant false advertisement[/u]:

[quote]
Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it.
[/quote]

If I stated what I consider my qualifications for knowing what constitutes "Hollywood-style" hacking, nobody would believe me, so I won't.  But even if you have never seen either a vtty or Hackers, I feel like anyone looking at the animation for the command called "porthack", god and the command name itself, and how it works, and everything related to the actual process of hacking (kinda the core concept in the entire game)... well I just think it doesn't take an expert to realize it's about as unrealistic as you can get.  If you don't believe me and this matters to you, buy the game and try it.  You will know I'm right within the 2 hour window to return it for a full refund, I assure you.  There is no "SSHCrack", no "FTPBounce", these wouldn't be PE executables if they did exist, PE doesn't even run on UNIX, "opening ports" and having requirements for a certain arbitrary number of open ports to "porthack" is very Hollywood.  Stahp.  Hollywood-style hacking is fine, don't be ashamed of it!  But most importantly, [b]advertise this game for it's many strengths, not for a falsehood[/b].  This game doesn't need lies to make it sound good, it's already a good game.  It's already a [i]great[/i] game.  Don't make false claims that sour its image.

Ok, now for the big one (to me).  Some people, many perhaps, won't care about this but I care.  I am quite literally sick to my stomach right now.  This has perhaps very minor spoilers for a very small number of optional (so far where I am in the story) missions, so I will spoiler-tag a lot to be safe, but even if you haven't played the game and hate spoilers, you probably won't be upset for reading the spoiler-tagged text in the next paragraph, it's the mildest of mild spoilers.

So, some of the missions require you to access a database of [spoiler]death row records[/spoiler] and modify them.  The missions are fine, and the topics are relevant.  I thought this was a positive thing to include in the game... until I gained access to this database and actually started reading the records.  I read about 40 of them in a row, unable to stop.  These were not made up, they were real records.  They had to be.  Surely the names were changed at least, right?  I Googled one at random and sure enough it was entirely real, and even the name, age, and date matched.  The [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] were their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler], verbatim.  There is literally a massive database of actual real people's [spoiler]deaths[/spoiler] including their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] in the game, and there are missions to modify this database!  It is making light of a very serious topic with real people's real, actual names, turning it into a game.  If I am [spoiler]executed[/spoiler], I don't want my [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] to be made into a fun, "cool" game.  That's awful!  These families are mourning!  Please do not take real, actual tragedy and juxtapose it alongside comical IRC chat logs!  In a game?!  If you are a U.S. company, the families of these people may have legal justification to press charges.  I almost hope they do.  But instead of that, I would rather you modify your game and replace the real data with artificial data that you make up, or at least change the names and please also [spoiler]their last words[/spoiler].  This would have been such a cool set of missions, with a positive political message, but since you used real data it ruins the whole thing and instead makes it a mishandled slog of insensitivity... or... words, I just hate that you used real data for this.  Please replace it with artificial data.  It won't hurt the game.  It will take a single developer a day, if that, and then you can be on the right side of things, morally and honestly probably legally.  I plan to ask my lawyer his opinion on this sometime when he's not busy, not to press charges myself (I'm not listed in the data), but just out of legal curiosity if charges could be pressed for something like this.

Anyway this is a fun game and I'm not going to try to refund it, I'm not even going to stop playing it, but I will stop recommending it or buying it for more people (I have a tendency to buy games I like repeatedly for lots and lots of people, friends, family, etc.).  I think I bought Necesse 12 or 13 times?  I also fully plan to modify this review if my issues are addressed.  I will do so as soon as I notice the changes.  If you reply to this review when you've addressed them, I will likely notice faster and therefore update it faster... you know, if you don't want one nerd girl's negative review.

TL;DR: Great game, super fun.  But it uses false advertising on its Steam page, and is horribly insensitive to real mourning families IRL, and doesn't even change the names.

-- Amy

It was fun and helpful to see some things I recognize from real life, such as the default system port numbers being accurate and the existence of a few UNIX commands (my main OS has been FreeBSD for years, and my experience with UNIX helped with the gameplay in a way that felt good). I liked seeing the C# source code and realizing it was actual, real C# source code that would probably work if the LESS_THAN was properly changed to a "<" sign, etc (C# is my main dev language, always a plus to see it referenced in a game at all). That was cool, and I'll probably compile it later to have that tool on my PC for real (don't comment about the related real life security to this -- I assure you I already know, and it's just for fun). The pacing was really good, and I got hooked fast. So fast that I immediately bought the DLC, soundtrack, and DLC soundtrack for myself, then bought the game and DLC for both my wife and her boyfriend also. Despite my negative review, I don't regret this decision at all, it's a very, very fun game. Oh, the event thing that I can't discuss without giving spoilers, but well, the one where you need to get that thing back, that was super fun! (Unimportant to the review and a spoiler:) I instinctively [spoiler]jumped to my host and forkbombed, apparently I was supposed to kill his forkbomb instead, oh well... I had already made a backup of that file just in case[/spoiler]. But anyway, the game was extremely fun, looks great, the music is great, and I'm excited to keep playing and see where things take me. But there are two issues which were severe enough that they prompted me to leave a negative review despite all this. The first issue isn't so bad and is easily rectified: This game is the pinnacle of Hollywood-style hacking. It does it very well, and it references real hacking concepts in the game's flavor text and other areas. Some tools are named the same as real ones, and you will probably learn a few real UNIX system port numbers, but that's about where the realism ends. Oh, and [b]this wouldn't bother me in the slightest[/b] -- I love Hollywood-style hacking sim games! -- but it clearly says this in the "Features" section in the game's Steam page description, which to me is [u]blatant false advertisement[/u]: [quote] Real Hacking Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it. [/quote] If I stated what I consider my qualifications for knowing what constitutes "Hollywood-style" hacking, nobody would believe me, so I won't. But even if you have never seen either a vtty or Hackers, I feel like anyone looking at the animation for the command called "porthack", god and the command name itself, and how it works, and everything related to the actual process of hacking (kinda the core concept in the entire game)... well I just think it doesn't take an expert to realize it's about as unrealistic as you can get. If you don't believe me and this matters to you, buy the game and try it. You will know I'm right within the 2 hour window to return it for a full refund, I assure you. There is no "SSHCrack", no "FTPBounce", these wouldn't be PE executables if they did exist, PE doesn't even run on UNIX, "opening ports" and having requirements for a certain arbitrary number of open ports to "porthack" is very Hollywood. Stahp. Hollywood-style hacking is fine, don't be ashamed of it! But most importantly, [b]advertise this game for it's many strengths, not for a falsehood[/b]. This game doesn't need lies to make it sound good, it's already a good game. It's already a [i]great[/i] game. Don't make false claims that sour its image. Ok, now for the big one (to me). Some people, many perhaps, won't care about this but I care. I am quite literally sick to my stomach right now. This has perhaps very minor spoilers for a very small number of optional (so far where I am in the story) missions, so I will spoiler-tag a lot to be safe, but even if you haven't played the game and hate spoilers, you probably won't be upset for reading the spoiler-tagged text in the next paragraph, it's the mildest of mild spoilers. So, some of the missions require you to access a database of [spoiler]death row records[/spoiler] and modify them. The missions are fine, and the topics are relevant. I thought this was a positive thing to include in the game... until I gained access to this database and actually started reading the records. I read about 40 of them in a row, unable to stop. These were not made up, they were real records. They had to be. Surely the names were changed at least, right? I Googled one at random and sure enough it was entirely real, and even the name, age, and date matched. The [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] were their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler], verbatim. There is literally a massive database of actual real people's [spoiler]deaths[/spoiler] including their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] in the game, and there are missions to modify this database! It is making light of a very serious topic with real people's real, actual names, turning it into a game. If I am [spoiler]executed[/spoiler], I don't want my [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] to be made into a fun, "cool" game. That's awful! These families are mourning! Please do not take real, actual tragedy and juxtapose it alongside comical IRC chat logs! In a game?! If you are a U.S. company, the families of these people may have legal justification to press charges. I almost hope they do. But instead of that, I would rather you modify your game and replace the real data with artificial data that you make up, or at least change the names and please also [spoiler]their last words[/spoiler]. This would have been such a cool set of missions, with a positive political message, but since you used real data it ruins the whole thing and instead makes it a mishandled slog of insensitivity... or... words, I just hate that you used real data for this. Please replace it with artificial data. It won't hurt the game. It will take a single developer a day, if that, and then you can be on the right side of things, morally and honestly probably legally. I plan to ask my lawyer his opinion on this sometime when he's not busy, not to press charges myself (I'm not listed in the data), but just out of legal curiosity if charges could be pressed for something like this. Anyway this is a fun game and I'm not going to try to refund it, I'm not even going to stop playing it, but I will stop recommending it or buying it for more people (I have a tendency to buy games I like repeatedly for lots and lots of people, friends, family, etc.). I think I bought Necesse 12 or 13 times? I also fully plan to modify this review if my issues are addressed. I will do so as soon as I notice the changes. If you reply to this review when you've addressed them, I will likely notice faster and therefore update it faster... you know, if you don't want one nerd girl's negative review. TL;DR: Great game, super fun. But it uses false advertising on its Steam page, and is horribly insensitive to real mourning families IRL, and doesn't even change the names. -- Amy

I bought this game on sale, only paid a few bucks for it, and still feel a little ripped off. This possibly could be turned into a good game, but I doubt they'd make the effort. It feels kinda like it's not complete. I actually quit the game in frustration after they got what proxies do blatantly wrong. They paint proxies as some sort of more advanced firewall.
This could be a fun game. I actually like the idea of a terminal simulator hacking game. It seemed kinda cool. That's why I bought it. But it's not fun. The writing is poor, though there are a few humourous references to a few things, like Harry Potter for example. They didn't even bother to get a lot of common common technology right. Why are you using exe's in *nix environments? This is definitely Hollywood hacking. Worse yet, it's Hollywood script kiddie-ing. It feels like a game that could be thrown together very quickly by a small group of coders. Worse yet, they apparently have a very limited understanding of computers.
If they fix all the areas that are blatantly WRONG, and do a few bug fixes so the commands work more like terminal commands, and make the writing a bit more compelling, it might make for a good game. As it stands, I've played it once, and I don't know how soon I will again. It feels like a few bucks down the drain.
Oddly enough, I keep getting the urge to play a game like this, but then I remember how bad this was when I did play it.

despite my playtime as of the review, ive enjoyed the game. its great! in my opinion, worth the price. sure, it has its vices, what game doesnt? the game isnt realistic to real life hacking, but i think its hard to make a game thats realistic and fun when it comes to hacking and/or programming games as it will be only for a specific audience which reduces who would play and enjoy the game by alot. its a bit repetitive with how hacking to most systems is the same, but i enjoyed many puzzles that this game provided, especially in the labyrinth DLC. this game isnt perfect, no game is but id say its honestly the closest of any games of this genre that i played. the music is one of the few game soundtracks that i actually liked and would listen to in my spare time. the multiple times that arent just port openers are fun and useful!... well most of them (looking at you, Clock.exe). but id say that some are underused, like the log creator and opener, theyre required to be used i think 2-3 times, but the gap between their uses is too big which makes those tools easily forgettable and can make some puzzles hard to impossible without googling how to solve them. id also say that the map can sometimes be hard to use with time, as if youre looking for a specific server, its hard to find it due to there being so many, even with the map organiser tool provided in the labyrinth DLC. i also love how the trace mechanic isnt an immediate game over like in other hacking games where there are also traces, instead you get a saving grace thats (in my opinion) too easy to complete once youve done it once as the process doesnt change if you need to do it many times. i also love how you can use either the GUI or visual part to play the game or the terminal, you are rarely forced to use either. the many customisation options are very fun and well made, they give you a fresh look at your game, either just changing how it looks to where some things are placed. and then theres the story, now im not an emotional personal and ill admit, i havent cried at the ending but i loved it and felt sorry for our favorite guy, especially after the ending cutscene. i had to replay the game to realise that what he meant is that the remaining copy is ours, the actual game. the labyrinth dlc also messes with the games directory, i would have loved to see more of this mechanic but i more than understand why it isnt used as it would likely get annoying. i also really like how there are what i presume are steam keys, i doubt there are any unredeemed keys after 8 years so i dont know what the keys are for, but its a nice gesture. the dev speaking to us after completing the game and letting us know the ips for some fun servers like "cheaters stash" basically letting us get most binary files (port openers and trace stopper) and others. the labyrinths ending is definitely an unexpected twist and while the choice doesnt matter its still nice to have one. i also immensely enjoyed the labyrinth DLC (if you havent noticed already), i enjoyed how the mission and hub actually looked like and the addition of letting us communicate with the others despite our inability to speak. it could also potentially be used if there was a multiplayer, like a race or trying to speedrun many preset missions, either trying to help or stall your friends and you could communicate as a nice feature, maybe making info on server1 vital to help solve a puzzle on server2 or something like that. also the amount of secrets or easter eggs there are is a very nice and fun addition. the shells are imo underused and their trap is rarely used, i think i used it like once or twice on my second playthrough and it actually did something. and there are the fan made DLCs which is great, you can still play even after you complete the actual game.

In short: i enjoyed the game very much, the characters (which are unfortunately few) are lovable. the game has its vices but those are few and often just mild annoyances. ill definitely be replaying the game and its DLC aswell as the fan made ones. its worth its price, but if you think its not for you, you can wait for a discount.

I believe this review to be my first, and let me say this: Hacknet is the most fun I've had with a piece of interactive media in a very long time. It oozes with immersion and masterclass functionality. After Portal 2, most people were left wandering aimlessly along the dunes of the puzzle genre. From time to time, there was an innovative incorporation of puzzle-elements, but never something so powerful. 

GNU/Linux is a UNIX-based mobile, server, office and home desktop operating system. It is built on the powerful and lightning-fast Linux kernel developed by Linus Torvalds in 1996. It's destiny was to maximize productivity and hasten the process of technological evolution. Being lightweight and monolithic, you can take Linux with you wherever you go. When you thought of the internet, you always heard about Linux ever so briefly. 

But recently, things have begun to change. As the corporation gains more control over what we've known to be the internet, people are becoming more concerned. The people want more control over what they rightfully own. Linux offers a full computer suite capable of doing everything a Windows system can do in its own way. This makes Linux a functional choice for people looking for a way out. 

To see such a beautiful piece of technology incorporated into a hacking simulator is beautiful. It's all done so faithfully too. The more I play, the more excited I get. It's fluid, only ever needing so much RAM to operate smoothly. It's also quite responsive, despite some animations taking a lot longer than they should honestly. Another minor flaw is the fact that there's no currency system. There's really only ranking as a reward. It would be cool to make some money and purchase upgrades or better tools.

My final gripe is that some of the missions get a little repetitive. But the story balances things out by keeping it all fresh. There will be funny conversations you can find throughout each system. There's also interesting hide-and-seek style treasure hunts. Listening to cyberpunk playlists really help bring the vibe forward. The interface is extremely realistic.

There was no need to go any further, everything is heavily inspired by an actual personal home desktop Linux installation. The desktop environment in this game gives me an i3-gaps vibe. I could be wrong. I'm just playing this on Linux and being amazed and how honest it feels. 

I wish you could change the wallpaper, the colors, and maybe even the font of your interface. It would make the game feel more personal and exciting. Imagine hacking on a cute hello kitty desktop! <3

[h1] Hacknet [/h1]
[b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b]

[h1] Run-through [/h1]

Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web.

With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

• Amazing story
• Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up
• Challenging and entertaining puzzles
• The music feels always on point with the situation
• Mod support
• Tons of fun little Easter Eggs

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

• The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre
• As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences

[h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1]

[u][b] General information [/b][/u]
Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job.

Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere.

There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth.

Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program.

The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games.

Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there.

[u][b] Content [/b][/u]
Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay.

[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]

[u][b] Graphics [/b][/u]
A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else.
Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text.

[u][b] Music [/b][/u]
For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions.

[u][b] HUD [/b][/u]
The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable.
To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other.

[u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u]
None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done.

[h1] Wrapping up [/h1]

Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for.


[h1] RATING: 8.5/10 [/h1]

However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay. [h1] Technical Analysis [/h1] [u][b] Graphics [/b][/u] A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else. Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text. [u][b] Music [/b][/u] For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions. [u][b] HUD [/b][/u] The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable. To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other. [u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u] None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done. [h1] Wrapping up [/h1] Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for. [url=https://kinglink-reviews.com/2018/05/21/hacknet-review/] Full Review [/url] --  [url=http://store.steampowered.com/curator/31803828-Kinglink-Reviews/] Curator Site [/url]

Hacking games are weird. There are games with hacking as an ability such as Deus Ex or Watch Dogs but that’s not what I’m talking about. Those game have a “hacking mechanic” which at best is a mini-game and at worst is a button press. There are also games where the focus is on “hacking” systems and while it’s almost never realistic it usually can take steps in that direction and still be fun. Hacknet is one of those games, and it is an excellent example of why I enjoy those games.

So there are two sets of games I play. Normal games, stuff like Far Cry, Destiny, Bayonetta that average gamers can enjoy the same as me. Then there are the special games. I call them “programmer games” And they’re not all the same, they don’t have the same style of gameplay but most are made for the analytical mind of a programmer. Programmer games to me are games like Factorio, and pretty much every Zachtronics game (Which I will start reviewing soon, I promise, Zach your day will come!). And Uplink. Yes, Uplink is certainly there.

Uplink might be the first game I ever played where I felt a bond with the developer. I didn’t just like Uplink. I loved every minute of it. I was a novice with computers (and in some ways maybe I still am) but Uplink gave me the feeling that I was hacking into computers, and racing to beat a trace to avoid detection. Uplink was a blast. It was a great game. Hell in the back of my mind whenever I’m running a route trace (tracert) or pinging a server, I still imagine the map of the world and believe it’s following a single line on it.

I’m not the only person who liked Uplink. I can say that with absolute certainty because Hacknet clearly was developed to be similar to Uplink. Now two people can come up with the same idea, but Hacknet came out a decade after Uplink and even has a mission about someone copying “Introversion’s” game idea in Hacknet. Introversion is the name of the company that made Uplink.

Because of that, I’m sure the question comes up if this is a clone. While I have a very long version of why it doesn’t matter, the question would carry more weight if Hacknet didn’t differentiate itself from Uplink, or if Uplink was still developed. Introversion has gone on to make other amazing games, including the current “Prison Architect”. While Uplink is a clear inspiration, it’s also just the starting point, and Hacknet ran with it in so many directions that I’m impressed.

But there is one thought that Hacknet didn’t improve on Uplink. Uplink has a rather solid story, and it’s exciting from the first moment to the end of the game. I remember playing it a number of times, and the story drove me on to finish it in more than one way.

Hacknet, on the other hand, has a weaker story. Most of the story is done through missions and while there are some choices the player can make, or choose between a number of groups, there’s not really a reason or a purpose for it.

The real story of Hacknet only appears at the end and it only becomes a major event for a number of missions in a row, but it’s never has a strong pull to finish it, instead you just want to keep completing missions and because of that the story pulls you along. I feel like a lot of the story comes out of nowhere.

That’s not to say there are no interesting stories in Hacknet, but they’re more about the current mission you are on or just side stories that develop the world. It’s a shame because it’s one of the big flaws in the game in my opinion. The game feels like it tries to be open to the player making choices so it’s free-form but then backloads all the major story events to the end. I’d have loved to see the major story develop into emergency situations you deal with throughout the game and you could get the feeling you are competing against something even if you weren’t.

The bigger problem to me though is the story doesn’t tend to listen to the rules it has set up for its universe. You start the game and eventually join a hacking group. The first group are “White Hats” which means constructive hacking. They don’t exactly follow those rules, but while they can be destructive, they have a moral code that’s critical for them. It’s a good mantra to follow, and I like the idea of it.

The problem is the game never follows it up. In fact, a few missions are hollow when you realize there’s no positives or negatives for how you do jobs. The group might claim they’re “White Hats” and they told me to only delete what was necessary on one assignment. I trashed the computer and destroyed everything I could. The group never brought up my destructive nature. In fact, from that point onward, I found I could go against almost all the rules that the story developed for me.

For instance, Hacknet stresses deleting logs are important, and this was critical in Uplink. If you left logs in Uplink, people would be able to backtrace you even after you disconnected. However, in Hacknet there are two problems. First disconnecting from a server leaves a final log entry that’s deadly. In real life, you could wipe the log, have a program delete them after a timed execution or crash a server to avoid writing a disconnect if it matters. But none of these are required because of the second issue. Leaving the logs alone makes no difference. It’s a story element that doesn’t actually have gameplay attached to it.

I want to say both of these are acceptable and they are, but in fact, they annoy me a lot. The logs were a core system in Uplink and while the new game doesn’t have to be exactly like Uplink, Hacknet talks about deleting logs as critical. If they make it a major part of the story, they should require it since they said it was important.

So this has started to evolve into a discussion on the gameplay, and the gameplay is either the best part or the worst part of Hacknet. It will pretty much come down to the question of if the player can use a terminal effectively.

If you take a random server in Hacknet, you’ll usually be presented with a login prompt and the ability to “probe the network”. Almost always you will have to probe the network, from there the game will tell you what type of security measures the servers have. It might be a proxy server that you have to overload with other servers or a Firewall that means there’s an analysis program you have to run and figure out a passcode by reading off the letters that remain after analysis. You’ll almost always have to open ports on the system so you can crack the password, and you open ports by running exploits. Almost all of this is only done through the console. You can probe with the mouse, but the exploits require running the programs manually and giving them the ports.

The thing is, this is rather fun to me. I love the hacking aspects, and eventually when there’s a time limit it gets even better, trying to get everything done against a ticking clock because you have to run all the exploits, overload the proxy, figure out the firewall, and then do whatever you intended on the computer before it locks you out again.

The downside is the trace is always the same length of time. In Uplink there’s an idea of proxies which worked, as you could build a longer trace time but here, you just directly attack the computer and either have enough time, disconnect before you’re finished or run out of time.

I didn't enjoy this game much at all. I like the idea of playing a hacking simulator, but the execution really fell flat. The challenges are monotonous and uninteresting. The files added in for flavor are tired-old jokes. There's not much in the way of story. And the interface is awful. The worst part is the network map where you connect to hosts, which is a crowded bunch of unlabeled dots that you just have to remember, (I eventually gave up and put the list of hosts/IPs into a text document on a second monitor so that I could at least hide the ones I thought I was done with) but the terminal and RAM screens are both pretty bad too. The RAM screen is a combination of an arbitrary hurdle and an excuse to add silly hacker media trope animations, and I want to know what program spends 300MB of ram displaying a short text file. The terminal doesn't scroll or even have history, so once some output goes off the top of the screen it's lost. Did you cat a file and not bother to read it until after rm /log/*; dc;? Have fun breaking back in to get the file again since a bunch of "Deleting file" messages pushed it off the screen? Did you want to !solve because you didn't get everything you wanted the first time you broke in? Too bad.

Definitely not worth the price or your time.

review_text_raw:
I'd only recommend this game if: you get it for free or really cheap, you want a short game to play but don't care what, or you just really want to see lots of scrolling lines and feel like a faux hacker

Otherwise, I don't think it's worth your time for the following reasons:

1. too simple and repetitive
Once you figure out the command lines after a few minutes that's the entire game play. In fact, you'll have to type the same things over so many times you'll mostly use the GUI menu instead. Then, you just wait around all the time waiting for the same 4-5 port hacks to finish that's nothing more than progress bars and flashing numbers like you see in movies. You do this again and again over the next few hours doing simple contracts you pick up from the hacker group postings board (which don't require any thinking since they tell you exactly where to go and what to do which is most of the time just deleting some files off the target server). 

2. lack of story and immersion
As mentioned above, 90% of the time you are doing these simple job postings. The other 10% is the actual story but other than a quick introduction to the missing dead hacker in the beginning, all of its related missions are shoehorned at the end in like the last three missions. Also, another problem I had was the immersion. If you read the files in the folders they want you to target, they're related to the back story of the mission you're doing but if you poke around in the home folder they're just a bunch of random files. For example, it doesn't make sense to read irc chat logs of teenagers making dumb pun jokes and a grocery list in an enterprise server.

3. some poor ui choices
Every IP address you visit is pinned on a board as a node that you can revisit at anytime. However, the nodes become very cluttered towards the end of the game, and critical story nodes at the end are overlapped with a bunch of nodes you visited at the start of the game. I got stuck for a bit for one mission because when I scanned for connected networks I could not see the one out of the five that newly showed up which I needed to go to. It really didn't help that the countdown timer (active trace, which I'll talk about below) was right on top of that region, blocking my view. Lastly, there's something about the background and font color choice and or the font size that is eye straining and made me feel nauseous at times. Made me want to skim through the text a lot of the times.

4. feature bypass/abuse
There's a gameplay feature called active trace which is basically a countdown timer before the server tracks you down because it knows it's being hacked. Fun idea in theory but it's only ever a threat once in the game. Every other time you can circumvent it by hacking the server then disconnecting, then when you reconnect you can login as admin because it saved the password somehow from just hacking the ports. At this point you can leisurely scroll through the server and not worry about getting caught. If you do run out the timer and get caught you go into fail safe mode where you have a limited time to change your ip address but I just rebooted the virtual OS and that "solves" the problem.
