It really didn't help that the countdown timer (active trace, which I'll talk about below) was right on top of that region, blocking my view. Lastly, there's something about the background and font color choice and or the font size that is eye straining and made me feel nauseous at times. Made me want to skim through the text a lot of the times. 4. feature bypass/abuse There's a gameplay feature called active trace which is basically a countdown timer before the server tracks you down because it knows it's being hacked. Fun idea in theory but it's only ever a threat once in the game. Every other time you can circumvent it by hacking the server then disconnecting, then when you reconnect you can login as admin because it saved the password somehow from just hacking the ports. At this point you can leisurely scroll through the server and not worry about getting caught. If you do run out the timer and get caught you go into fail safe mode where you have a limited time to change your ip address but I just rebooted the virtual OS and that "solves" the problem.

review_text_raw:
I have never left a review here in on steam for anything....that in itself should make you appreciate just how strongly I feel about what I am about to say and just how absolutely and unequivocally true what I am about to say really is.

Let's start from the positives.....actually positive:
The graphics are OK....along with the music it does create an atmosphere appropriate to the setting of the game.
That's it.

READ THIS BEFORE YOU BUY:
1) The game is essentially a mishap collection of dubiously formatted XML files, along with the main executable of the game which is obviously just a parser along with the graphics engine (presumably). Although it is possible to play the game normally, I guarantee that you will soon waste your time trying to "fix" the myriad of issues that arise from the poor structure of the gameplay itself (more on that later) See my play time? 87 hours? Most of it has been spent scouring the internet on ways to fix broken missions, enable progression through other parts of the story, etc.
2)There are several limits to and aspects of the basic design that make NO sense. For example, yes, you can use a "terminal" with a few commands to progress through the game. These commands include options to open and close your actual CD tray (wow, how ARG of the author--when was the last time anybody used the CD tray for anything? when was the last time anybody saw a computer with an actual CD drive ???). HOWEVER IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO CREATE OR DELETE DIRECTORIES IN YOUR IN-GAME COMPUTER, NOR CREATE FILES..That's right....as crazy as it sounds, you can't even copy files on your own machine. The only way to create files is downloading them from somewhere else and then renaming them if you want to "fake" a simple copy command....but yes, if you want a game that opens your CD tray by all means, stop reading this now and buy the game. The terminal itself has no ability to scroll up, which sometimes means you need to retrace your steps if you forgot to jot some key piece of information down.
3)There is no hardware upgrade system, which means your hacking machine is what it is from beginning to end. It doesn't really matter for the most part, as the speed of the operations you perform in the game is largely dependent on your own ability and response time (that's the main game mechanic). However RAM is kind of important, because that's what all your hacking tools consume to run, as expected. The problem is that if you, for example have the notes app open with passwords and information about your current mission (thus avoiding the aforementioned backtracking in point 2) , you will run out of memory pretty quickly...forcing you to run programs one at a time and wishing you could actually make money in this game to buy more than 1 GB of ram (lol...seriously...just lol).
4)You can only accept 1 mission at a time (WHY...JUST WHY?!???!). This may not seem a big issue, but it is what literally breaks the game again and again. This ridiculous limitation means that you can't complete all the missions offered in the game because no matter what you do as you progress through the story the game forces you to move on and leave the unfinished missions behind, never to be played. The only way to get past this is to go and edit your save game (you guessed it, an XML file) in order to make it possible to complete some missions (this fix doesn't always work btw). This becomes a huge problem close to the end of the story. Without spoiling anything, you end up having two missions to do, and it seems that it doesn't matter the order you do them in, but if you choose wrong a subsequent mission will be skipped entirely (it is one of the most notorious bugs of the game) and you will miss part of the narrative and context. Seriously, if you are thinking of buying this game, in order to enjoy the story as it was meant to be played, you should first look up what I have just told you and figure out which mission you should do first when you get to that juncture, or be prepared to restart the whole game if you mess up (unbelievable).
5)The least the author could've done was to include a save management system, but of course, there is none. If you want to make sure you don't have to restart the game in case something gets screwed up (see above) you must manually backup your savegame file, and you have to be careful too...because although the game doesn't autosave normally it will autosave in certain circumstances, barely warning you that this has been done.
6)Although the game never crashes, there are a few technical bugs that wouldn't even be a problem if not for everything that i mentioned above. When working with the terminal, using the arrow keys to edit a command sometimes doesn't work properly, and there are a few other such things (sometimes, for example, you have to hack a computer twice because although you were able to hack in the first time, the game doesn't register it). There are also a few grammar mistakes that again, not really important on its own but if added to all of the above, it's just the "cherry" on top that you don't want...especially from a paid game, however cheap it is. 
7) There is a ranking system, but it doesn't work. No matter how many missions you complete and how high your rank is according to the success emails you get at the end of each completed mission, you are still the last on the list, with 0 points. It's annoying. Suggestion to the author: if a feature is too hard/you are to lazy to implement...don't include it, especially if it has no bearing on the gameplay whatsoever. It is pretty disappointing to reach the end of the game and see that in the eyes of your hacking faction you are still a newb. 

Now....I get it, it's an indie game...what did I expect? Well I expected something a little more functional. As a software developer myself I understand a few of the choices the author made, but sill...there are some laps in basic human logic that are beyond me. For example, it is obvious that is technically more difficult to write an "open world" style game as opposed to a linear game play experience. That's why the player is allowed to play one mission at a time. I really get it. What I don't get is if a linear game is what you wanted to code...THEN DO NOT OFFER CHOICES TO THE PLAYER THAT YOUR GAME IS UNABLE TO SUPPORT AND FORCE HIM/HER/THEY TO START OVER!!!
I also understand that is hard to test a piece of software by yourself, I have done it as my main occupation for many years. A few bugs are bound to crop up...but hey...IN THE CREDITS THERE ARE MENTIONED A WHOLE SLEW OF TESTERS...what the heck did they test exactly? Seriously...I want to see what test cases they ran on this....

I would ask for a refund...but hey if didn't get my 60 bucks back from CD Projekt RED for Cyberprank 2077 I certainly won't ask the 5 bucks i spent on this (i got the DLC too). Go ahead, enjoy your Starbucks latte on me.  
According to the author, this game started out as a 48h game jam project and was later refined for 2 and a half years to become what's on steam now. 2/3 YEARS??!?!?! THIS IS WHAT YOU COME UP WITH? I think the best definition of this game is just that....a barely interesting project  hurriedly cobbled together  for a 48h game jam event.

tl;dr; Do yourself a favor and buy Uplink Elite, which is obviously what this game wanted to be and failed...miserably. I'd be willing to gift Uplink to the author as well so that he can see how a game like this SHOULD be made.

Hacknet is a cyberpunk-themed hacking simulation game that places players in the role of a hacker tasked with completing various digital missions. Dive into the world of computer systems, uncover secrets, and navigate a web of challenges in a realistic and immersive experience. The game blends puzzle-solving, strategy, and a deep narrative to keep players engaged.

[b]Key Features:[/b]

[b]Hacking Simulation:[/b] Hacknet offers a unique and authentic hacking experience, where players utilize a variety of commands and tools to infiltrate systems. The realistic simulation of a hacker's environment adds an extra layer of depth and immersion.

[b]Narrative-Driven Gameplay:[/b] The game features an engaging story where players uncover a conspiracy as they hack into various systems. The narrative unfolds through emails and logs, enhancing the sense of mystery and intrigue as the player progresses.

[b]Puzzle-Solving Mechanics:[/b] Each mission in Hacknet presents complex puzzles that require players to think critically and use their skills. The puzzles become progressively more challenging, adding a sense of accomplishment upon completion.

[b]Cyberpunk Atmosphere:[/b] Hacknet captures the essence of a cyberpunk world, with its gritty visuals and electronic soundscape. The game's aesthetic is minimalistic but effective, contributing to the overall tension and immersion.

[b]Realistic Hacking Tools:[/b] Players are equipped with a variety of hacking tools and software that mimic real-world techniques. The need to learn and adapt to new tools and strategies is a key aspect of the gameplay.

[b]Time-Sensitive Missions:[/b] Players must act quickly to complete missions before their actions are detected. This adds an element of urgency and excitement to the gameplay, pushing players to work efficiently under pressure.

[b]Conclusion:[/b] Hacknet stands out as an immersive and engaging hacking simulation game that captures the essence of a cyberpunk world. Its narrative, puzzle-solving mechanics, and realistic hacking tools provide a captivating experience for players who enjoy strategy, problem-solving, and an atmospheric gaming environment. The game's unique approach to hacking and its strong narrative make it a memorable experience in the cyberpunk genre.

review_text_raw:
[b]Hacknet[/b] is a hacking simulation game. You are probably familiar with other games of the same genre, such as Uplink and the Hacker Evolution series. This game is, I dare to say, better than both of those, despite having some bugs.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.

[h1]What is happening in the game:[/h1]
Fourteen days after Agent Bit's disappearance, a failsafe sequence was activated. You are one of the only people who can solve Bit's death. As you get more and more involved into the hacker community, you start unveiling a mystery and it's up to you to discover what was really behind Bit and the security system he created.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]After the success of Uplink, there had to be a game sooner or later that would try to improve what Uplink started. Hacknet not only achieves that, but takes it to the next level. The story alone is amazing and makes sure that you're not just repeating the same commands and actions over and over but gives it a meaning.
    [*]I have to say that the whole interface is working really nicely when it comes to clarity and effectiveness. You can do 90% of things both in the Display section and Terminal section, but they are both placed in the interface and I find it surprisingly effective. I use the Display section for figuring out what is going on and the Terminal section to execute commands.
    [*]You have a nice map on the bottom of the screen, that is showing all of the cyber locations you have visited already. As you get to connect to tons of computers, you would think that the map would be overcrowded, but this is not the case. I found the map really useful, despite it being almost completely covered.
    [*]There is no bouncing from servers as you remember from other hacking games. Instead, traces are lost if you simply disconnect. Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge.
    [*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job.
    [*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal.
    [*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful).
    [*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did.
    [*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that.
    [*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want.
    [*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly.
    [*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine.
    [*]This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files.
[/list]

[h1]The final verdict:[/h1]
As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive.
This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast!

Greetings,
BirdCute

Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge. [*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job. [*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal. [*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful). [*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did. [*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that. [*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want. [*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly. [*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist. [/list] [h1]Cons:[/h1] [list] [*]Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine. [*]This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files. [/list] [h1]The final verdict:[/h1] As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive. This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast! Greetings, BirdCute [quote]Note that my copy of this game was obtained for free for reviewing purposes. However, this did not affect the quality and objectivity of this review.[/quote]

review_text_raw:
[h1] INTRO [/h1]
The best way to describe Hacknet for me is that it's an experience. You will like it if you're curious about what you see in the trailers and on YouTube. The comparison to real hacking that I've seen around the Interwebs is there in the similarities with the commands that you type into a terminal window, and the use of I.P. addresses, but that's really about it (Read about that here: https://www.quora.com/How-closely-is-HackNet-OS-game-related-to-the-real-life-hacking). But besides all of that, you should give it a go. It's $15, and it was worth every dime. I'll go into details below about why, but I would blanket recommend this game if you've seen anything interesting in the trailers, reviews, or content about this game. 

[h1] BEGINNING [/h1]
I'll go chronologically here: I found this game in a weird way. I found Furi through Dunkey's Best of 2017, and while listening to the Soundtrack for it Payload came on thanks to shuffle. I'll get to the soundtrack a "Bit" later, but Payload is one heck of an advertisement for Hacknet. The developer Matt Trobbiani said that the tutorial was what he was most proud of, which comes right when you start a New Session (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=suQ_dT8ucVg 0:52). I found that it was... lacking. I was unsure of how to solve most problems at the beginning of the game that I was presented with, and the convoluted explanations of what the commands did was not helpful for knowing what exactly to do with them. My examples here are the explanation of Shells and an Executable that I can't remember. If you're anything like me, the first hour(s) will be a grind: learning the commands, getting a feel for what the missions are asking of you, and learning the flow of the game. [i] Note: I found that saying what's wrong plainly will help with finding a solution. For example: "My file got deleted, I need another one. I'll just go and steal it". [/i] This was my challenge, and I found myself on the incredibly helpful Steam guide more than a few times in the early game (DO NOT USE THIS UNTIL YOU ARE STUCK https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=499723234). This was a more sufficient tutorial for getting accustomed to the game and progressing. But that's just the beginning of the game, and the game's biggest fault in my opinion. 

[h1] MID GAME [/h1]
After my mixed experience with the beginning of the game, things got better, and quickly. After you know the commands well and how they are used, (shell, rm, probe, connect, addnote, append/replace, upload, and a few more basics) you start to see the timing the game expects of you. The Trace adds real intensity to the game that will the expanded upon later. It really gets exciting as the commands come naturally to you. I disagree with Matt about the success of the tutorial, rather I would praise him on the pacing and creativity of the mid and the beautiful, beautiful, oh so beautiful endgame. I found myself going back to the guide less and less, and realizing that most problems can be solved with basic knowledge of the game, and a curiosity for combing through systems. You've got to look carefully through everything. You'll find everything from weird conversations to passwords that you can't proceed without. The flow of the mid game is quite enjoyable as the difficulty slowly picks up and your Net Map gets bigger and bigger. You start to get the sense that Hacknet is an open world game, which it is. Hacknet takes you through the mid game and cleverly prepares you for the final challenges that you will be ready for if you've paid attention throughout the game, and you won't have to use any guides at all. 

[h1] ENDGAME [/h1]
Hacknet's final challenge is daunting, but well-designed. Now for the ending. I won't say too much because it is best experienced without expectation, but I will say that it made it all worth it. Learning the commands, how the game is played, it all comes together. In a rather mild game, the experience of the ending is quite "shocking". This was where Hacknet was completely untouchable. I would give any amount of money to go back and experience that ending for the first time again. Best part of the game, by far. Sequencer is my favorite Executable and it will be yours as well once you finish the game. Now to the soundtrack, because this section and the next one go hand-in-hand. 

[h1] MUSIC [/h1]
Now I'm a music guy, and the soundtrack plays a huge role in Hacknet's overall experience. That's because there are almost no sound effects, the beeping of the Trace timer, accepting and competing contracts, and an Incoming Signal are all of the ones I can think of right now. If you turned the music off in settings, the game would be silent. Therefore there is a huge emphasis on the soundtrack. And I'll just say that I'm listening to Roja Drifts By just to get in the spirit for this section. There's a few really good ones, and the rest are ok. Here's a list of the good stuff: Carpenter Brut for obvious reasons, Tetrameth, Roja Drifts By, Outrun the Wolves, and in Labyrinths Dream Head, and even the legendary Resonance makes an appearance (at one point Matt said he thought he wouldn't make enough money to pay the artists back). The rest of the soundtrack was nice and "techno-y" and perfectly fit with the theme of the game and what you see on your screen. But the standout for me was obviously Remi Gallego. Everything he's put out, especially for Hacknet and Labyrinths turned out to be some of my favorite songs ever. Payload, Panic Track (which is basically Malware Injection), ClearText, and Sabotage were all masterpiece songs. I encourage you to check out the work he did on Hell is Other Demons as well if you liked his stuff here, it's great. However mentioning Payload gives me the opportunity to talk about the one problem that Hacknet has with its use of the soundtrack. I know Payload appears in Labyrinths, but the problem occurs in the main game as well. The songs are just set to repeat until you complete a contract or two (I also did not appreciate Matt cutting out the glitching in Payload, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4l6arwAIA6w 4:03). It gets old, and I found myself muting the music for a while to keep all of the tracks fresh because they are reused at points. 

[h1] STORY [/h1]
Lastly I'll touch on the story here, it's good. There's a Bit of a twist as to the fate of Hacknet which I thought was really cool, but it was also a bit convoluted. Took me some reading afterwards to figure out what just happened, but that's also because I wasn't really paying attention to the story and more worrying about why I couldn't complete some mission. Let's just say it's not spelled out, but I guess some players understood it pretty easily (THIS IS A STEAM FORUM ABOUT THE ENDING AND EXPLAINING IT, I AM ONLY INCLUDING IT TO SHOW THAT THE ENDING IS EXPLAINED IF YOU LOOK FOR IT https://steamcommunity.com/app/365450/discussions/0/530649887207612803/). Anyways, the story is strong and interesting, but you don't play it for the story. It's interesting enough that you could, but you just don't. 

[h1] SUMMARY & RATING [/h1]
Overall an unforgettable experience. Easter eggs, music, intensity, it's fun for the whole family (not really suitable for the whole family). Be patient in the beginning, learn the commands, comb through the systems, learn what is required of you. There are bumps and surprises waiting for you, and you're rewarded for jumping through each hurdle. Please give this a shot, I found music that I loved, an ending so good I pooped myself, I fought my way through an unfamiliar system, and I learned about video games. There's bound to be something you like about the game if you [b] stick with it [/b]. And if you liked what you played in the main game, get Labyrinths (https://store.steampowered.com/app/521840/Hacknet__Labyrinths/). You won't be sorry, mate. Matt put a lot of love into this game, and it shows. [b] 9/10. [/b]

Too naive for those are familiar with *nix. It's recommend to do the hack in real world to introduce people to *nix world. https://overthewire.org/wargames/ may be a better choice.

Let's talk about the process introduced in the game. How to scan the port? With nmap. And then? Nothing, just these four letters. What about the IP and port scan ranges? Too rough, the command should be accurate. No brain is involved. OK, now, we found the open ports, but all of them are locked, so how to hack in? Download an program from somewhere, and execute it. What?!!! How could you do that? It's so ridicules! Do you know who is that? How could you trust him without any thinking ? What if it is virus?  This is the reason that stop me from playing it anymore. Continuing talking about the hacking process, how to break the ssh port? Just type SSHhacker.exe like that of nmap. It is Sooooo boring.

Besides, the variety of commands is so poor. First, there are too few commands, you do not have find or something else. Second, the implement of existing commands are so rough: You cannot "rm *IP". You could only do "rm *" or delete one by one. For "cat" command, you could only "cat" the files under current directory, but cannot do that with directory prefix.

The reasons for not recommending are summarized below:

1. You cannot learn how to use the commands, and you may fill very uncomfortable with those naive commands.
2. You cannot learn the real hack. The name of the game is "HACKET", so what is hack? The "SSHhacker.exe" is. How to create the "SSHhacker.exe" is the key point.
3. You cannot learn safety consciousness, as said before.

review_text_raw:
I’m not entirely sure what to think about this game. I feel like this game had the potential to be a lot more interesting than it turned out to be. I did have fun with this game and thought some of the missions were interesting. But, I can’t really figure out what this game is trying to be and I came away with the feeling that this game isn’t really finished. 

In terms of hacking and the operating system, it’s fairly weak and, at times, frustrating. The hacking programs you run are basically magic in terms of how powerful they are. They work on anything and require no modification based on the target. The challenge comes from managing your bizarre computer’s memory system and timing attacks to avoid the hollywood-style ‘tracing’. The simplified hacking mechanics aren’t a bad thing, I think. Real hacking elements would make the game extremely complicated, tedious, and boring. 

But, that aside, there are weird limitations on what you can do and what exists in the world. The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done.

As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. 

The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos,  grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly.

I hate that there is no option inbetween the thumbs up and down, because I think the game is still fun. But, comparing how much I liked to how much I didn’t like, I have to give it a thumbs down. This game has great ideas, it just hasn’t fleshed them out enough.

review_text_raw:
The game design works at first, and there are timed missions when you really get into the action – musics do their job. You have kind of a sense of accomplishment as you get your hands on more "hacking" tools and get to face bigger challenges. There is quite a lot of humorous content on the side – not in the main story! – and that's appreciated because it's not far from being a text game.

But that's about all the nice things I can think about this game. Pretty soon, you reach its limits and the sense of accomplishment fades away. If you have no feeling for IT stuff, you may get lost pretty fast. But if you're too much into it, the game mechanisms are very disappointing. The main idea was good, but the execution rather bad. If you're still curious, I'd suggest to buy it on sale.

The difficulty relies on: 1. The cryptic aspect of computers – you'd better know the basics about file system and console ;  2. Timed challenges ; 3. Finding little bits of information (user name, password, IP...) here and there among text in files and mail ; 4. Systematically scan the targets in all ways possible. That's not something that keeps one entertained for long.

The console, which you use a lot, is rather rudimentary. At the very least it should have felt like a real one and at least to go smoothly when you type. The cursor is glitchy, not always showing where it actually is. Key pushes may be repeated when hold a few microseconds too long. The number of commands is very limited. They are sometimes buggy when not used as intended. Managing the in-game files is pretty tedious, there are no commands for creating/deleting directories. There is no way to make scripts or shortcuts. At best you can rename the executables. By the way, having "exe" files on a Linux simulation is an heresy.

The graphic interface lacks functionalities too. It would be great if you could move and resize the panels, especially the one for the "netmap" which gets pretty packed and hard to read after a while. You may find an in-game executable which helps a little bit with that. Also content will overflow from panels when too big. Why no copy/paste available?!? It would have been so useful. I grew tired of retype every user name, password and IP. Plus there are some links that are meant to be open in a real browser (as eater eggs only).

The game mechanisms are very limited. Some special missions or events break the monotony, but the player are not prepared for them either. [spoiler]For instance you are not likely to be able to defend your computer against other hackers.[/spoiler] The hacking tools are also limited in number, in versions and they almost all work in the same way. Missions are quite alike, and you're doing the same dull things over, and over, and over...

They tried to make up for it with the game story, but it turns out to be a bit déjà vu, corny, and even a bit predictable.

Two alternatives would have been preferable for making such a game:
— Either make it more approachable, even less realistic but with a more pleasant game design. Then it would need hacking to be more like puzzles.
— Or make a game for nerds, where the in-game computers can be configured, where files matter, with better console commands and executables, even maybe some scripts to edit.

review_text_raw:
Wow, Hacknet is one immersive command line game.
You get to pick up the left overs of a now dead hacker, following in his footsteps, slowly taking on harder challenges and making a name for yourself.
Hacknet offers a tight narrative (which is completely text based) and enthralling 'hacking'

Pros:
 - presentation. I know a lot of people will be turned off by a CL interface game. but heck (huehue), it's beautiful, intuitive and well designed. plus you can download more UIs from servers and people you hacked
 - gameplay. it's relatively easy, requiring (so far, I'm roughly 4 hours into the game) simple management skills, a keen eye and some reading and prioritizing. the hacking is served well, not letting you button mash, but rather focused on the finer points such as: reading emails for usernames and passwords, changing websites headers into vulgarities, finding the right tools and balance, covering your tracks.
     a lot of the gameplay is indeed done over a command line interface, which, exactly, means you type out what you wanna do. there's helps, and little tools making it a lot easier than real life hacking could ever be.
- Story. it's a pretty cool mix of paranoia, technology and a weird form of justice. no one talks, no fancy cutscenes. it's all in your head, buddy
 - immersion. yeah, the computers you hack are rather empty, but what is on there is hilarious and often gives small hints to connections between the hackers you 'meet' (I think, at least
 - music. absolutely perfect. 

Cons:
 - uhm, let me think ... hmmm ... no, it is exactly what it says it is. and then some

Verdict:

You like hacking/hacking movies or just recently discovered Mr Robot or the deep web?
Well, come on in. this is a perfect supplement to your diet.
Hacknet is pretty (for CL standards :D as I work in IT I actually find it gorgeous), fun and fast paced. It will test your patience, but mostly your ability to read and type properly.
But nothing is keeping it from delivering the best hacker game since Uplink, if not even a tick better.
And it is totally worth the price tag

review_text_raw:
[b]Hacknet[/b] is a hacking simulation game. You are probably familiar with other games of the same genre, such as Uplink and the Hacker Evolution series. This game is, I dare to say, better than both of those, despite having some bugs.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.

[h1] What is happening in the game: [/h1]
Fourteen days after Agent Bit's disappearance, a failsafe sequence was activated. You are one of the only people who can solve Bit's death. As you get more and more involved into the hacker community, you start unveiling a mystery and it's up to you to discover what was really behind Bit and the security system he created.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]After the success of Uplink, there had to be a game sooner or later that would try to improve what Uplink started. Hacknet not only achieves that, but takes it to the next level. The story alone is amazing and makes sure that you're not just repeating the same commands and actions over and over but gives it a meaning.
[*]I have to say that the whole interface is working really nicely when it comes to clarity and effectiveness. You can do 90% of things both in the Display section and Terminal section, but they are both placed in the interface and I find it surprisingly effective. I use the Display section for figuring out what is going on and the Terminal section to execute commands.
[*]You have a nice map on the bottom of the screen, that is showing all of the cyber locations you have visited already. As you get to connect to tons of computers, you would think that the map would be overcrowded, but this is not the case. I found the map really useful, despite it being almost completely covered.
[*]There is no bouncing from servers as you remember from other hacking games. Instead, traces are lost if you simply disconnect. Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge.
[*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job.
[*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal.
[*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. [*]It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful).
[*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did.
[*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that.
[*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want.
[*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly.
[*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine.
This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files.

[h1]The final verdict:[/h1]
As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive.
This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast!

This was Kedeajan,
Have fun!

review_text_raw:
[b]DISCLAIMER: I was provided a press review copy for the purposes of documenting the game for PCGamingWiki, a publicly-editable technical wiki for games.[/b]

What would happen if you gamified the idea that you found a copy of an OS which was so dead-simple to use, anyone with basic computer and investigative skills could hack into [i]anything[/i]? You'd get Hacknet, an excellent hacking game designed to be the spiritual successor to Uplink. Slick graphics, a sliding difficulty designed to get you introduced to the game's mechancis one-by-one, and an in-the-background story which is surprisingly pointient and explores not only how insecure computers really are to a dedicated hacker, but the ramifications, both practical and mornal, of an OS designed to hack anything.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] It's a short, satisfying hacking game which, despite how complicated it seems at the outset, eases you into its mechanics, world, and story, and gives you the surprising, satisfying feeling of being both a master hacker and Sherlock Holmes at the same time.

[h1]Is this Uplink 2.0?[/h1]
For the mandatory "Is this Uplink 2.0" part of the review: no. This is [i]not[/i] the spiritual successor hardcore fans of Uplink have been looking for because:
[list]
[*] You use a 'real' computer with fixed specs, with HacknetOS running on top of it as a VM (Virtual Machine).
[*] The game is command-line based with some GUI helpers, such as an IP map, optional GUI-based system navigation, and a note app.
[*] You can only run computer-compromising apps via command-line.
[*] The game's story, despite being subtle, in the background, and without limitations (i.e. x number of connections before game over), drives the game, and your actions are ultimately in service of the story.
[/list]

If none of the above scared you off, then read on because this spiritual sequel is, in spite of the above, a worthy one IMO...
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As mentioned above, Hacknet uses its command-line for much of the hacking, with a few GUI helpers for those tasks too cumbersome to exclusively do in the GUI, like keeping track of all the known IPs and keeping notes. Despite this, there are only a few core commands, and are remarkably easy-to-remember with repeated use - and the game is [i]very[/i] careful to ensure you do - and often relate to what they do. For example, to crack an in-game computer's SSH port, run SSHcrack [insert port number here]. This is further helped by the addition of command auto-completion - something the game teaches you how to use very quickly. So, that SSHcrack command I just mentioned? All you really need to type in is SSH, press the TAB key, add the port number, and press the Enter key. Believe me - it makes your life a [i]lot[/i] easier.

The hacking itself is simple: connect to the target, probe the computer for weaknesses, then execute programs to exploit their weaknesses. Some computers require some preperatory work, such as computers with proxies effectively require you to use other computers you've compromised to attack them, while others might require you to find a piece of cracking software to open them up, bypass a firewall by running special software to solve its encryption, and so on. At first, it isn't so difficult - just run the apps, and watch the magic happen. Later on, you'll begin to regularly encounter computers which will attempt to passively hunt your computer down and force it to reboot - complete with a giant timer showing you the exact time to failure - requiring you to run multiple apps at once. Since your computer only has so much memory, you'll need to play Tetris with the apps, shutting down those you don't need and running the ones which bypass the easiest weaknessess. Beating the clock and compromising a computer with a second to spare is an accomplishment in an of itself which never gets old.

Another good thing is the game understands how counter-intuitive command-line use is for the average user, so through the use of an initial tutorial (which can be skipped once you know how to terminate it) and missions which slowly slide up in difficulty as they teach the basic mechanics, you'll eventually come to grips with the commands you need to hack. And once you do, it starts giving you missions which, combined with the clear, clever visuals (more on those later), allow you to feel like a master hacker in a way different from other hacking games because you'll often need to do something which most hacking games leave out entirely or towards the very end.

[b]You get to be Sherlock Holmes.[/b]

You see, because people, even those with good security sense, tend to forget or excuse security issues, they also tend to leave stuff on their computers, mobile devices, and e-mail accounts. IP addresses to secret files, administrator (admin) passwords for top-secret servers and their most private e-mails - you name it, they'll leave it. As such, any good hacker needs to dig through files to find all those details so they can find what they need with the least amount of effort - allowing you to find hidden servers, open files which would otherwise be closed to you, and skip dangerous, time-consuming, and sometimes impossible system hacks by simply logging in as the administrator. You'll be surprised how satisfied you'll feel following a trail of clues to your ultimate objective, making an impossible task suddenly seem trivial - and end up finding some hilarious stuff in the process as you dig through all the files which don't matter.

All that said, there are some things which make the game easier than it should be. A key part of the gameplay is erasing anything in the system's logs indicating you were there so the authorities can't track your hacks back to you. In theory, this means deleting every log file before leaving the server; in practice, all you have to do in most cases is start deleting all the log files, disconnect from the server, wait for all the files to be deleted, then come back. "How can I delete files from a computer I just disconnected from?" you ask. You shouldn't, but the game lets you. This means that as long as the computer doesn't have a rotating admin password - and most don't - what should be down-to-the-wire hacks end up being trivial. Furthermore, any future accessing of the computer will be ignored - even if you never delete the logs after the first time.

Oddly enough, that one problem with the gameplay is...actually a bonus in my eyes, since it enables you to focus more on solving the challenging Sherlock Holmes-esque puzzles.
[h1]Story[/h1]
I can't really touch on the story much as to do so would ruin the surprise and horror it provides late in the game. I can say, though, that the story, while simple, is quite sophisticated, as it explores through your actions just what kind of power HacknetOS gives those who own it in today's digital age, where everything - and I do mean [i]everything[/i] - is connected to the Internet and, thus, can be compromised, pried open, and tampered with.
[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The graphics in Hacknet are very minimalistic and clean, meaning you can see exactly what's what with minimal effort. There are also some optional, subtle effects which emulate a CRT computer monitor, adding to the realism. The standout graphics come from the apps, as they show you in fun and clever ways how they're progressing, whether it shows you punching through an SSH table with every section hacked turned green or beat out an SMTP mail server's sorting algorithm to force it to shut down and open up to you.
[h1]Additional Thoughts[/h1]
I really wish the game opened up towards the middle - it would've been fun exploring the world wide web, finding hidden sub-plots as you tear through the world's computers like tissue paper, as a reprieve from the short story. Speaking of the story, I also wish it were longer - the game's puzzles were clever and unique, and I so desperately wanted more content.

All you really need to type in is SSH, press the TAB key, add the port number, and press the Enter key. Believe me - it makes your life a [i]lot[/i] easier. The hacking itself is simple: connect to the target, probe the computer for weaknesses, then execute programs to exploit their weaknesses. Some computers require some preperatory work, such as computers with proxies effectively require you to use other computers you've compromised to attack them, while others might require you to find a piece of cracking software to open them up, bypass a firewall by running special software to solve its encryption, and so on. At first, it isn't so difficult - just run the apps, and watch the magic happen. Later on, you'll begin to regularly encounter computers which will attempt to passively hunt your computer down and force it to reboot - complete with a giant timer showing you the exact time to failure - requiring you to run multiple apps at once. Since your computer only has so much memory, you'll need to play Tetris with the apps, shutting down those you don't need and running the ones which bypass the easiest weaknessess. Beating the clock and compromising a computer with a second to spare is an accomplishment in an of itself which never gets old. Another good thing is the game understands how counter-intuitive command-line use is for the average user, so through the use of an initial tutorial (which can be skipped once you know how to terminate it) and missions which slowly slide up in difficulty as they teach the basic mechanics, you'll eventually come to grips with the commands you need to hack. And once you do, it starts giving you missions which, combined with the clear, clever visuals (more on those later), allow you to feel like a master hacker in a way different from other hacking games because you'll often need to do something which most hacking games leave out entirely or towards the very end. [b]You get to be Sherlock Holmes.[/b] You see, because people, even those with good security sense, tend to forget or excuse security issues, they also tend to leave stuff on their computers, mobile devices, and e-mail accounts. IP addresses to secret files, administrator (admin) passwords for top-secret servers and their most private e-mails - you name it, they'll leave it. As such, any good hacker needs to dig through files to find all those details so they can find what they need with the least amount of effort - allowing you to find hidden servers, open files which would otherwise be closed to you, and skip dangerous, time-consuming, and sometimes impossible system hacks by simply logging in as the administrator. You'll be surprised how satisfied you'll feel following a trail of clues to your ultimate objective, making an impossible task suddenly seem trivial - and end up finding some hilarious stuff in the process as you dig through all the files which don't matter. All that said, there are some things which make the game easier than it should be. A key part of the gameplay is erasing anything in the system's logs indicating you were there so the authorities can't track your hacks back to you. In theory, this means deleting every log file before leaving the server; in practice, all you have to do in most cases is start deleting all the log files, disconnect from the server, wait for all the files to be deleted, then come back. "How can I delete files from a computer I just disconnected from?" you ask. You shouldn't, but the game lets you. This means that as long as the computer doesn't have a rotating admin password - and most don't - what should be down-to-the-wire hacks end up being trivial. Furthermore, any future accessing of the computer will be ignored - even if you never delete the logs after the first time. Oddly enough, that one problem with the gameplay is...actually a bonus in my eyes, since it enables you to focus more on solving the challenging Sherlock Holmes-esque puzzles. [h1]Story[/h1] I can't really touch on the story much as to do so would ruin the surprise and horror it provides late in the game. I can say, though, that the story, while simple, is quite sophisticated, as it explores through your actions just what kind of power HacknetOS gives those who own it in today's digital age, where everything - and I do mean [i]everything[/i] - is connected to the Internet and, thus, can be compromised, pried open, and tampered with. [h1]Graphics[/h1] The graphics in Hacknet are very minimalistic and clean, meaning you can see exactly what's what with minimal effort. There are also some optional, subtle effects which emulate a CRT computer monitor, adding to the realism. The standout graphics come from the apps, as they show you in fun and clever ways how they're progressing, whether it shows you punching through an SSH table with every section hacked turned green or beat out an SMTP mail server's sorting algorithm to force it to shut down and open up to you. [h1]Additional Thoughts[/h1] I really wish the game opened up towards the middle - it would've been fun exploring the world wide web, finding hidden sub-plots as you tear through the world's computers like tissue paper, as a reprieve from the short story. Speaking of the story, I also wish it were longer - the game's puzzles were clever and unique, and I so desperately wanted more content.

Cool Concept, But It Couldn’t Keep Me Hooked

Hacknet starts strong. The idea of diving into a terminal-based hacking sim with a mysterious narrative hook is instantly appealing, especially if you’re into cyberpunk aesthetics or want to feel like a digital detective. At first, typing out real commands and navigating the virtual systems feels immersive and fresh. But that feeling didn’t last long for me.

The main problem is how quickly the novelty wears off. After a couple of missions, the gameplay loop becomes repetitive — scan, probe, crack, read a few emails, rinse and repeat. There’s little variety or meaningful evolution in the mechanics. You’re not solving clever puzzles so much as going through the motions of the same routine over and over.

The story, while intriguing in concept, never really grabbed me. It’s told in fragments through logs and emails, but it lacks emotional weight or urgency. I never felt particularly invested in the characters or their motivations — and a lot of the writing just felt flat.

On top of that, there are some pacing issues. Some tasks feel tedious and drawn out, while others jump ahead abruptly. And if you’re not already familiar with basic command-line structure, the early learning curve can feel more frustrating than fun.

I really wanted to like Hacknet. It nails the aesthetic and tone, and I respect the ambition. But the shallow gameplay and underwhelming story made it feel more like a tech demo than a fully satisfying experience.

review_text_raw:
1. You can't finish all contracts. At some point the game will just tell you "You're good enough for more difficult tasks" and a main quest will trigger, blocking you from accepting new quests. You can never go back and you can't do them after the final mission.

2. You can't create files or directories. Organizing your downloaded files is annoying because you can only use the pre-defined ones. In one contract you're supposed to forge a file, and that works by downloading a file and editing the copy...

3. You can't remove directories. There's almost never a need to do so, but when you need to remove the contents from a directory with multiple subdirectories, you need to access each subdir individually and remove the contents.

4. Autocomplete doesn't add a whitespace after the autocompleteted word. Confusing as hell for a regular terminal user.

5. The final mission consists of multiple phases, which each one explaining your next goal. In phase 3 you're supposed to send a password but you aren't told so. I just used the password I found to login and continued my quest. After a while I got stuck, and after more than an hour I finally looked into a walkthrough - and learnt that I needed to send the password instead of entering it, and that had already solved the final mission by myself over an hour ago. At least I could just click the "complete quest" button 4 times in a row to trigger the ending.

6. The gameplay is quite repetetive. Connect to a server, open the closed ports (which always works the same, for all of them), find the file you need. There are only 2 missions that go beyond that and actually force you to think: The final mission, and the mission before. That doesn't really speak for the game.

7. The map is just plain awful. It's cluttered with nodes from earlier contracts which you never need to connect to anymore. Literally hardest part of the game is finding the correct node on the map.

8. Secrets. Don't get me wrong, secrets are great. But I looked into a guide after finishing the game, and some secrets didn't trigger for me although I definitely satisfied their conditions. So maybe I shouldn't have written "Secrets", but "Bugs". Furthermore, some secrets get you hyped, and when you finally solve their puzzle, you get... a digital clock that even uses up your RAM?

9. Alt+Tab closes the game.

I completed the game in a single session. It was kinda fun, although way too easy. But damn, some of the issues I just mentioned are pissing me off and I'm not going to play the DLC or any user-created mod.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a game about hacking. The game opens with the Hacknet OS booting up with a message from a man named Bit, who says that if you see the message, he’s already dead. He leads you on a quest to start hacking, getting the attention of one hacker group, then a second, all to avenge his death and prevent the distribution of a hacking program.

The story itself is kind of mediocre, but it is serviceable; at its core, it is a story of corporate greed, as well as a revenge story, though by the end of it, it is pretty clear that the whole thing isn’t really as sinister as it appeared at first.

The real core of the story is the hacking – you log into various computers, break through their security mechanisms, and then are lead onto other computers. Spicing things up are timers, various mechanisms you have to bypass, and the various files and passwords and IPs you have to find to lead you on the next leg of your hunt.

Sadly, the game is plagued with poor design decisions. There are various points at which it isn’t clear what you’re supposed to be doing, and you’re left confused, only to find out you needed to hit the “reply” button on an email after breaking into a server to move on – despite the fact that the email wasn’t clear about that. At other times, you have to send them messages, and while this is usually clear (sending them an IP or password), on occasion it is not and ends up being rather frustrating.

Worse (and even more frustrating) are some outright bugs – situations where the game simply does not function like it is supposed to. Beyond there being some lost forevers in the game which are less than obvious, there’s additionally the fact that sometimes the game simply bugs out and won’t let you progress or do various things. You get a “mission incomplete” message when trying to proceed, and there’s simply no clear way around the issue. Indeed, two of the achievements require you to do things which simply don’t function half the time or more, judging by the many frustrated players who had to restart the game time and again to try and get them to work.

The UI itself is a bit obtuse at times as well; several of the hacking programs you use require additional bits of typing to execute, despite the fact that in many cases it literally never matters – it is always exactly the same number you have to punch in. And while it is neat seeing it use actual hackerish commands, ultimately there’s a lot of little pieces which just feel annoying to have to do time and again.

The only real good thing about the game is its aesthetics; which do work pretty well for what it is.

In the end, you aren’t really rewarded for your frustration. The core idea is cute enough, but in the end the game ends up being rather repetitive, and there just isn’t enough variation in the core gameplay. A mediocre story combined with sometimes unclear gating mechanics to make the game advance is just not a winning recipe for a game.

The game seems like a neat idea at first, but it just ends up being more frustrating than enjoyable to play. It isn’t worth your time or your money.

After completing Hacknet and it's Labirynths expansion I believe that the game is worth experiencing for the price it asks.

The Good:
- 8h campaign (I did some NOT ALL side missions and the Labirynth expansion)
- Interesting storylines
- Moral Disconnect/Dilemmas
- Simplicity                                   < Easy to understand, just a bit hard to remember commands etc.
- Workshop Support                     < People made some very awesome mods.
- Visuals                                        < It makes your screen look suspicious

The Bad:
- Simplicity
- Slightly difficult to navigate "network map" < Yes I am aware of the existence of the sorter. I still think it could be better in some way.

My wishlist:
- More complexity in the puzzles.
- Clearer more understandable map.
- More ways to solve objectives.
- Hardware Customisation.

Conclusion:
A very pleasant experience with possible extension via the mods on the workshop. Decent story with some interesting twists. The hacking gameplay becomes quite repetitive with time, as it just requires you to think what tool to use for each port. The investigative gameplay is actually surprisingly fun, the game leaves you with enough hints to go on, however the game rarely offers a situation to decide the outcome or change the approach to completing objective. In a certain sense it is linear.

review_text_raw:
HACKNET - 7/10

Quick Review: A "hacking simulator" with gameplay akin to getting your first DOS system up and running, Hacknets weak story doesn't hold back the interesting and ever expanding gameplay.

Story
------
You, an amateur hacker, are contacted by someone named "Bit", who gives you an extra tool to add to your hacking repertoire and from there the expansive world is open to you. Using your new found tools, you become a part of something greater, helping (obviously shady) people with your hacking skills while trying to figure out just what the hell the Hacknet really is, and it might be more dangerous than you thought...

Overall, unfortunately the story is the weakest point. Everything is told through text in the game and the story really only starts to open up and become explained by the end but by that time you're more than likely burnt out from your constant reading. Most of the game has you completing irrelevant odd jobs for obvious scum with little relevance to the story, which is why the story is the weakest part.

Gameplay
-----------
Gameplay of Hacknet involves 2 things: typing and hacking. Your UI is a command window with a display of the target computer in the center, all the devices you have access to at the bottom and the command console on the right. Basic gameplay goes like this: Select a PC you want to hack, you "probe" it (by typing "probe") which will display a list of security measures. You then type whatever relevant command you need for the security measure (theres about 6 different types and you'll get the tools required as you progress through the game), wait a bit for it to be hacked, than do whatever it is the quest needs you to do; either copy a file to your system, delete a file, edit a file, find an ip address and send it to the client etc. The entire game revolves around typing commands and clicking files.

I do think the gameplay is fun however, it has to be for me to give it a 7/10. By the time you get the hang of your newly introduced command, you'll learn yet another and another until you get near the end. There is alot you can do and quite alot of secrets to find as you make your way through the story. The gameplay at it's core is simple but it takes a while to memorise all the power you have.

Design
-------
The UI for the game is great, and the gameplay experience really makes you feel like H4CK3RM@NZ.  You get access to different coloured themes as you progress, and alot of the files you can find on the computers are quite hilarious. The soundtrack is a banger too, and the end of the game features some of the best final music i've ever heard.

Problems
----------
It's a simple game, so it has simple problems. Alot of the text files you find on computers are just copy pasted across many devices, filling them up so you spend more time browsing through them than needed. There was a bit too much waiting involved when it came to hacking and required almost 0 thought, you simply type the command for whatever hacking tool you need and the number that corresponds with it, then you wait. The biggest problem I have is that as you get further and further in the game, the amount of devices you can access starts to clutter your device map. Because devices are represented as circles with no names, I spent ages hovering over 30+ circles trying to find what computer I was looking for, and they end up overlapping sometimes too. This sometimes made me have to re-hack into a previous computer to find the IP for the computer I wanted to hack into even if I already had it available, simply because it was impossible to find on my device map.

Achievements
---------------
The achievements are....relatively easy and can be gotten in 1 playthrough but you need to know what to do without the game telling you. You need to discover quite a few secrets and go out of your way to get alot of the achievements but there isn't an enormous amount of content in the game so as long as you try and explore everything you'll probably get them.

Summary
----------
A super unique experience and nothing like i've ever played. The banging soundtrack and addictive gameplay makes me easily recommend this, but only if you can overlook it's numerous, but not awful problems.

Also I can't stress enough the end of the game. It's seriously, SERIOUSLY amazing and worth playing just to experience it. Everything about it is great and the song that plays alongside it couldn't have been more perfect...for anything.

I do think the gameplay is fun however, it has to be for me to give it a 7/10. By the time you get the hang of your newly introduced command, you'll learn yet another and another until you get near the end. There is alot you can do and quite alot of secrets to find as you make your way through the story. The gameplay at it's core is simple but it takes a while to memorise all the power you have. Design ------- The UI for the game is great, and the gameplay experience really makes you feel like H4CK3RM@NZ. You get access to different coloured themes as you progress, and alot of the files you can find on the computers are quite hilarious. The soundtrack is a banger too, and the end of the game features some of the best final music i've ever heard. Problems ---------- It's a simple game, so it has simple problems. Alot of the text files you find on computers are just copy pasted across many devices, filling them up so you spend more time browsing through them than needed. There was a bit too much waiting involved when it came to hacking and required almost 0 thought, you simply type the command for whatever hacking tool you need and the number that corresponds with it, then you wait. The biggest problem I have is that as you get further and further in the game, the amount of devices you can access starts to clutter your device map. Because devices are represented as circles with no names, I spent ages hovering over 30+ circles trying to find what computer I was looking for, and they end up overlapping sometimes too. This sometimes made me have to re-hack into a previous computer to find the IP for the computer I wanted to hack into even if I already had it available, simply because it was impossible to find on my device map. Achievements --------------- The achievements are....relatively easy and can be gotten in 1 playthrough but you need to know what to do without the game telling you. You need to discover quite a few secrets and go out of your way to get alot of the achievements but there isn't an enormous amount of content in the game so as long as you try and explore everything you'll probably get them. Summary ---------- A super unique experience and nothing like i've ever played. The banging soundtrack and addictive gameplay makes me easily recommend this, but only if you can overlook it's numerous, but not awful problems. Also I can't stress enough the end of the game. It's seriously, SERIOUSLY amazing and worth playing just to experience it. Everything about it is great and the song that plays alongside it couldn't have been more perfect...for anything.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very unique genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. [/h1]

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc.

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it.

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into.

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into.

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

This game is just like UPLink with better GUI.

[b]Cons[/b]
Gameplay is pretty repetative, terminal simulation is just awful:
[list]
    [*] The command are real, but they don't behave the real way. Why 'mv myFile myFolder/.' not only moves the file but also renames it??
    [*] Wildcard is used only when it is not surrounded with char, so no way to use 'rm myFile*' to delete both 'myFile1' and 'myFile2'. It just says 'No such file'
    [*] Tab-autocompletion worked better in Nokia 3310 than here. It works only in the top level, so no autocompleteion when you type 'cd folder/<TAB>' which made me actually traverse thru every folder, instead of going right where I needed to.
    [*] Why the hell 'scp' instead of 'cp'???
    [*] We're in UNIX world, and all our 'hacking' tools have 'exe' extension... Really???
[/list]

[b]Pros[/b]
The idea is interesting, there are a lot of pieces of different information scattered around the servers. I really like the idea of typing commands instead of clicking with the mouse. Nice idea with mimicing to 'man' :)

[b]Overall[/b]
Nice game, with a bit repetative gameplay. The game was killed by stupid terminal implementation.
But authors, really, RTFM... or at least support wildcards and dots properly in your terminal...
